For knee osteoarthritis, a Cochrane review (Manheimer et al., 2010) found small pain improvements, below the threshold of clinical relevance compared with sham acupuncture, and the NICE guideline NG226 (2022) does not recommend acupuncture for osteoarthritis. For acupressure the evidence is limited; the basis of treatment remains exercise, muscle strengthening and weight loss.

For hot flashes (low certainty), acupuncture has limited and inconsistent evidence; some studies show small improvements compared with no treatment, but less so compared with placebo acupuncture. Acupressure is a comfort adjunct.

For depression, the evidence for acupuncture is of low quality and inconsistent; for acupressure alone there is no solid evidence. It does not replace psychotherapy or medical treatment.

For primary dysmenorrhea, the Cochrane reviews (Smith et al., 2011 and 2016) show low-certainty evidence that acupuncture and acupressure may reduce pain compared with no treatment, with small studies and risk of bias; analgesics (NSAIDs) and heat have more solid evidence.
For knee osteoarthritis pain, the effect compared with no treatment is moderate, but compared with sham it is small and often below the clinical threshold.

For fibromyalgia, a Cochrane review (Deare et al., 2013) found low- to moderate-certainty evidence that electroacupuncture relieves pain and stiffness, but not that manual acupuncture is better than sham acupuncture. Gentle aerobic exercise and tai chi have more consistent evidence; acupressure is mainly a relaxation adjunct.

For nausea in pregnancy, the Cochrane review (Matthews et al., 2015) shows low-quality, inconsistent evidence for PC6 acupressure; a clear benefit over sham has not been demonstrated. Safety is considered good for PC6 in the existing studies, but their number is small.

For insomnia, the existing reviews show low-certainty evidence regarding sleep quality after acupuncture, with a high risk of bias; for acupressure, small studies show modest improvements. Cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is the first-line treatment (ACP 2016, AASM).

For chronic low back pain, a Cochrane review (Mu et al., 2020) shows that acupuncture (with needles) reduces pain compared with no treatment (moderate certainty), but compared with sham acupuncture the difference is small, below the threshold of clinical relevance (low certainty). The NICE guideline NG59 does not recommend acupuncture for low back pain; other guidelines (ACP 2017) include it as a non-pharmacological option. For acupressure alone the evidence is weaker; it may bring relaxation and comfort alongside movement and exercise.

For migraine prophylaxis, acupuncture has moderate-level evidence (Cochrane reviews) for reducing the frequency of attacks, at least similar in some studies to preventive medication, but with low-quality evidence; for acupressure the evidence is limited.

For allergic rhinitis, the Cochrane review (Feng et al., 2015) suggests a benefit of acupuncture, but with low- to moderate-certainty evidence, and the difference compared with sham acupuncture is uncertain; for acupressure the evidence is limited. It is not an alternative to antiallergic treatment.
For some symptoms (e.g. nausea, pain) the evidence is limited to moderate; there is no evidence that acupuncture cures or prevents cancer.

The He-Sea points are usually located near the elbow or knee (for example LI11 and HT3 at the elbow). Those on the leg, called "Lower He" points, are traditionally linked to the Fu organs: ST36 (Stomach), GB34 (Gallbladder), BL40 (Bladder). The Hui (Influential) points are eight places that "gather" certain tissues or substances: CV12 for the Fu organs, CV17 for Qi, BL17 for blood, GB34 for tendons and muscles, BL11 for bones, GB39 for marrow, LU9 for vessels and LR13 for the Zang organs.

Rules of caution: avoid damaged, inflamed or rash-affected skin, visible varicose veins, areas with recent bruises and operated areas, as well as areas with venous thrombosis, recent fractures or tumors. In young children and frail elderly people the pressure remains very gentle. Do not press hard on the abdomen after a meal or in pregnancy without medical advice; some points (for example LI4, SP6) are avoided in pregnancy in tradition. Stop if dizziness, persistent numbness or increasing pain occur. Acupressure is comfort care and does not replace medical evaluation for new, intense or persistent symptoms.

Breathing is half of the technique. Inhale through the nose for a few seconds, and on the long exhalation increase the pressure slightly; on the next exhalation hold it. Calm breathing lowers muscle tension and makes the sensation easier to bear. In TCM tradition, slow exhalation helps "Qi to circulate"; in the modern explanation, slow breathing may favor activation of the parasympathetic system, and attention to the sensation may change pain perception.
Slow breathing may lower tension and favor the parasympathetic response; TCM describes it in terms of Qi, but the practical benefit is relaxation.

Studies show that the accuracy of point location varies between practitioners, and differences of a few millimeters are common. Some studies also suggest that the measured effects depend less on an exact point than on the area stimulated and the type of stimulus, but the question remains open. This calls for methodological modesty, not negligence: in a course, we strive to locate correctly, but we do not claim millimeter exactness.

Studies on acupuncture for sciatica are of variable quality, with limited evidence; the NICE guideline NG59 does not recommend it for low back pain with or without sciatica. Acupressure is at most a comfort adjunct.

TENS (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation) uses electrodes on the skin and low currents for pain. TEAS is the variant applied to acupuncture points. For TENS the evidence is mixed: some studies support benefits for pain, especially in certain conditions, but the quality of the studies is variable and the effect may be small. For TEAS, studies in the perioperative period and in other contexts are promising but heterogeneous. Contraindications: pacemaker, epilepsy (especially on the head/neck), pregnancy (specific regions), damaged skin, areas with tumors, the region of the heart and neck, areas with loss of sensation.

An important step was the Zhenjiu Jiayijing ("The Systematic A–B Classic of Acupuncture and Moxibustion"), compiled by Huangfu Mi in the second half of the 3rd century AD (c. 256–282). The author reorganized the older material into a systematic structure of points, locations and indications. It became a reference for centuries, and the locations in it decisively influenced the later tradition.

Emergency 112: dizziness with chest pain, weakness of the face or of a limb, speech or vision disturbances, severe headache, fainting, suddenly developed difficulty walking, intense vertigo with vomiting and inability to stand, double vision. Dizziness with bleeding (including heavy menstrual bleeding), in pregnancy or with palpitations requires evaluation. See a doctor if the dizziness is recurrent, with vertigo or reduced hearing. Intense chest pain, or chest pain with sweating, shortness of breath or radiating pain to the arm/jaw is an emergency: call 112.

Emergency 112: the worst headache of your life or with sudden onset, new or prolonged aura, weakness or numbness on one side, speech disturbances, fever with stiff neck, after trauma, seizures. See a doctor if the migraine pattern changes or appears after age 50. Aura with hormonal contraceptives, pregnancy, or temple pain with vision disturbances require prompt medical evaluation.

Emergency 112: sudden and severe headache ("the worst of your life"), with fever and stiff neck, after trauma, with confusion, double vision, weakness, speech disturbances or seizures. It is also an emergency in the case of headache triggered by cough/exertion/sexual activity, with a skin rash with spots that do not fade on pressure, with a painful red eye and blurred vision, or in pregnancy/after childbirth with high blood pressure. Temple tenderness, pain when chewing or vision disturbances after age 50 may be temporal arteritis (risk of blindness): emergency. See a doctor if the headache is new after age 50, progressive, wakes you from sleep or changes your usual pattern.

Emergency 112: severe difficulty breathing, inability to speak in sentences, bluish lips, no response to rescue medication, confusion or exhaustion. Do not use acupressure during an attack. See a doctor if you need your rescue inhaler more often than usual or you wake at night with symptoms.

Do not force "cracking" maneuvers of the neck. In pregnancy omit GB21. Intense chest pain, or chest pain with sweating, shortness of breath or radiating pain to the arm/jaw is an emergency: call 112.

Emergency: intense or one-sided abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, fainting (possible ectopic pregnancy), severe headache with vision disturbances, vomiting blood. See a doctor if: repeated vomiting that does not allow hydration, weight loss, little dark-colored urine, dizziness, abdominal pain, bleeding, fever. Hyperemesis gravidarum requires medical treatment.

Emergency: shoulder pain with chest pain, dyspnea or sweating (possibly cardiac), after a fall with deformity, fever, red and warm shoulder, sudden loss of arm strength, drooping face or slurred speech (possible stroke: 112). Pain in the left shoulder or with a feeling of pressure in the chest may be cardiac: do not massage it, call 112. See a doctor also if the pain persists for more than a few weeks or wakes you at night.

Cupping creates a vacuum that slightly lifts the skin and tissues. A distinction is made between dry cupping (static, gliding) and wet cupping (hijama), where small superficial incisions are made and a little blood is drawn. The circular marks are ecchymoses (blood leaked under the skin), not open wounds, but they can last days or weeks; cupping is not applied on damaged skin, with anticoagulants, in pregnancy (abdomen and lumbar area) or on young children. Wet cupping involves a risk of infection, including transmission of blood-borne viruses, if the instruments are not sterile, so only with professionals who maintain strict hygiene. In 1822 (the second year of the Daoguang reign) acupuncture and moxibustion were removed from the Imperial Academy of Medicine; they remained in popular practice. The exact reasons are debated by historians.

In the app you will always see the same distinction: what tradition says and what studies support. Modern evidence is of low to moderate quality for some chronic pains (low back, headache, migraine) and for postoperative nausea, and the benefits are generally small; for knee osteoarthritis the difference compared with sham is small and often below the threshold of clinical relevance. For many other conditions the evidence is weak or contradictory. Studies with "sham acupuncture" often show small differences compared with real acupuncture, which suggests that part of the benefit comes from the context: attention, ritual, expectation and relaxation. This effect is real for the person who experiences it, but it should not be confused with a specific mechanism of the points.
